draft.title: Draft your criteria
draft.goal: Turn the five things you know into at least three criteria, each tied to a requirement and each marked as format or content.
why: A criterion is one thing a good answer must do. Writing them down before you look at any answer keeps your judgment fair, because you cannot bend the rules to fit what you see.
Each criterion traces to a requirement, so nothing is checked that nobody asked for and nothing that was asked for is forgotten.
You mark each one as format (how the answer looks) or content (what the answer says). A set with both catches a polished answer that misses the point.
The worksheet is this course's way of drafting. Other approaches work too, such as a list in a document.
instructions: Read the scenario and the five things you know. They are not in the rough notes, so a good answer has to meet them anyway.
Add a row for each criterion. Pick a requirement from the card, or write your own, then write the criterion in your own words.
Choose Format or Content for each row. Aim for at least three rows, with at least one about content.
Press Save my worksheet. Nothing is saved until you do.
Tick the two self-checks when they are true for your rows, then press Check my work.

scenario.intro: It is Friday afternoon and you need to send your project lead a short end-of-week update. You will use your AI tool to turn your rough notes into the update.

requirements.label: It is sent as a Teams message, not an email
The work is grouped by client (Northwind, Contoso, Internal), not by day
It calls out the blocker and what you need to resolve it
The tone is factual, not self-promotional

scenario.task: Your task: write at least three criteria that a good update must meet. Nothing is run in this Part. You only write the rules.

ticks.label: Each criterion traces to a requirement
No two criteria check the same thing

troubleshooting.problem: You are not sure whether a criterion is format or content.
troubleshooting.fix: Ask whether it is about how the answer looks (its length, its layout, how it starts) or about what it says (the facts and points it includes). If it is about what it says, choose Content.

troubleshooting.problem: Two of your rows seem to check the same thing.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep the clearer one and change the other so it checks something different, or remove it.

troubleshooting.problem: You cannot find a requirement for a criterion.
troubleshooting.fix: A criterion with no requirement behind it checks something nobody asked for. Pick a requirement from the card, or leave the criterion out.

troubleshooting.problem: Check my work says you have unsaved changes.
troubleshooting.fix: Press Save my worksheet first, then check again.

thresholds.title: Add a pass or fail rule
thresholds.goal: Give every criterion a threshold a script could decide, with no judgment needed.
why: A criterion says what to look for. A threshold says exactly where pass ends and fail begins. Without one, two people can read the same answer and disagree.
The script test keeps you honest: could a script decide this? If a person would have to judge, tighten the rule until a script could.
Some qualities cannot be checked with a rule. Say so with Not checked and a reason, instead of pretending.
instructions: Your rows from the last step are below, each with an empty Threshold box.
Write a threshold for each one that a script could decide: a number, a list of terms you choose, or a label the answer must carry.
If a rule cannot judge something, write Not checked: and the reason.
Press Save my thresholds. Read any notes that appear, and change a threshold if a note helps.
Tick the script test when it is true for every threshold, then press Check my work.

ticks.label: I applied the script test to every threshold: a script could decide it

vague.text: Row {n} uses {words}. A script cannot decide that as it stands. Try a number, such as a word count; a list of terms you choose; or a label the answer must carry. If no rule can check it, write Not checked: and say why.

troubleshooting.problem: You cannot turn a criterion into a rule.
troubleshooting.fix: Ask what you would look for with your own eyes, then write that down. If it needs your judgment every time, write Not checked: and the reason.

troubleshooting.problem: A note flags a word you chose on purpose.
troubleshooting.fix: Put the word inside quotation marks. Words in quotation marks are treated as terms you chose, so they are not flagged.

troubleshooting.problem: You want to change a criterion, not only a threshold.
troubleshooting.fix: Criteria are changed in the earlier step. After you build your file, you can also edit it there.

script_test.label: Script test applied
script_test.fail: Tick the script test once you have applied it to every threshold.

test-file.title: Write your test cases down
test-file.goal: Build a test case file from your worksheet, edit it, and make it pass the file checks.
why: A file holds your rules in one place, in a layout a person and a program can both read. Part 3 turns a file like this into a checker.
Writing the rules down before any answer is judged keeps a score honest.
The file is this course's way of recording rules. Other formats can hold the same rules.
instructions: Press Build my file from my worksheet. Your criteria, requirements, types and thresholds are copied in, in your own words.
Read the file in the editor. Edit anything that needs to change.
If a threshold points to a list, such as terms to avoid or terms that must appear, write that list under Supporting lists. Write your own: the app does not fill it in.
Press Save my file, then Check my work.

troubleshooting.problem: The build button says there is no worksheet.
troubleshooting.fix: Go back to the earlier steps and save your worksheet first.

troubleshooting.problem: You built the file and then lost your edits.
troubleshooting.fix: Building replaces the saved file, and the app asks first. Press Cancel to keep what you have.

troubleshooting.problem: Check my work says a criterion is missing.
troubleshooting.fix: Each criterion starts with a heading such as ### C1: and then lines for Requirement, Type and Threshold.

reference.title: Compare with an example
reference.goal: See an example set of criteria, and say how each one compares with yours.
why: You wrote your own rules first, so you can now see what an example does differently without it replacing your thinking.
Comparing shows where your rules were strong, where something was missed and where yours were too vague to check.
The example is one good answer. A different set of criteria can also be right, and this is not a score.
instructions: Read each example criterion next to your own file.
For each one, choose how it compares: you had it, you missed it, yours differs but works, or yours was too vague.
If you want to improve your file after comparing, edit it below and press Save my file.
Press Check my work when every example criterion has a choice.

troubleshooting.problem: None of the choices fits exactly.
troubleshooting.fix: Choose the closest one. The app does not judge your choices, and they are only for you.

troubleshooting.problem: Your file looks different from the example.
troubleshooting.fix: That is fine. Different criteria can also be right. Choose how each example criterion compares with what you wrote.
